name: COG7-congenital disorder of glycosylation (COG7-CDG, CDG type IIe)
aliases: conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 7 defect

clinicalPearls: COG7-CDG is an autosomal-recessive defect of the conserved oligomeric Golgi (COG) complex, a tethering complex governing intra-Golgi trafficking; loss of subunit 7 disrupts Golgi glycosylation machinery.
Unlike the ER-assembly type I CDGs, a COG defect impairs Golgi processing, so it is a type II CDG and characteristically shows a combined N- and O-glycosylation abnormality.
The transferrin pattern is a type 2 profile, and apolipoprotein C-III isoform analysis is abnormal, reflecting concurrent mucin-type O-glycosylation defect.
Presentation is typically neonatal and severe: profound hypotonia, failure to thrive, feeding difficulty, microcephaly and developmental delay.
Progressive hepatic involvement with cholestasis/hepatomegaly and cardiac dysfunction are important multisystem features.
Episodic hyperthermia and susceptibility to intercurrent illness with recurrent infections and increased early mortality are characteristic.
Dysmorphism, skin fragility/wrinkling and skeletal features may be present, reflecting broad glycoprotein hypoglycosylation.
COG7-CDG is one of several COG-subunit CDGs (COG1, COG2, COG4, COG5, COG6, COG8); recognising the group prompts targeted testing of the whole complex.
reference.pathophysiology: COG7-CDG is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in COG7, which encodes subunit 7 of the eight-subunit conserved oligomeric Golgi (COG) complex. The COG complex is a peripheral-membrane tethering complex that mediates retrograde vesicular trafficking within the Golgi and correct localisation of glycosyltransferases and nucleotide-sugar transporters. Loss of COG7 destabilises the complex and mislocalises multiple Golgi enzymes, so both N-linked glycan processing and mucin-type O-linked glycosylation are impaired; this combined defect during the Golgi (processing) phase makes it a type II CDG and produces the type 2 transferrin isoform pattern together with an abnormal apolipoprotein C-III profile. Because a wide array of glycoproteins depend on correct Golgi maturation, hypoglycosylation is generalised and multisystem, affecting the developing nervous system, liver, heart, skin and thermoregulation, which accounts for the severe neonatal encephalopathy, cholestatic liver disease, cardiac dysfunction, episodic hyperthermia and vulnerability to intercurrent illness.
additionalDifferentials: Other COG-complex CDGs (COG1-, COG2-, COG4-, COG5-, COG6- and COG8-CDG)
Other type II CDGs such as MGAT2-CDG, B4GALT1-CDG, SLC35A1/A2-CDG and TMEM165-CDG
PMM2-CDG and other type I CDGs (distinguished by transferrin pattern)
Neonatal cholestatic liver disease of other genetic or infective cause
Mitochondrial hepatoencephalopathies presenting in the neonatal period
Peroxisomal biogenesis disorders with hypotonia, dysmorphism and hepatic disease
Genetic syndromes causing neonatal hypotonia with dysmorphism and multisystem involvement
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry (expected type 2 pattern)
Apolipoprotein C-III isoform analysis to demonstrate the associated O-glycosylation defect
Molecular confirmation by COG7 sequencing, CDG/COG gene panel or exome/genome sequencing
Liver function tests, coagulation studies and cardiac evaluation (echocardiography) for multisystem disease
Brain MRI and electroencephalography for structural anomalies and seizures
Fibroblast/cell-based Golgi trafficking or glycosylation studies in specialist laboratories
Monitoring during febrile/intercurrent illness given episodic hyperthermia and decompensation risk
redFlags: Neonatal decompensation with severe hypotonia, feeding failure and faltering growth
Episodes of unexplained hyperthermia or rapid deterioration during intercurrent infection
Progressive cholestasis, hepatic failure or coagulopathy
Recurrent or severe infections in a hypoglycosylated, vulnerable infant
reference.prognosis: COG7-CDG is a severe multisystem disorder with high early mortality; survivors have significant neurodevelopmental disability and ongoing hepatic, cardiac and infective morbidity. There is no curative treatment, and management is supportive and multidisciplinary, with particular vigilance during febrile illness.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis by testing only N-glycosylation; the combined N- and O-glycan defect requires apolipoprotein C-III analysis for a complete picture.
Attributing a type 2 transferrin pattern to acquired causes without pursuing a Golgi-trafficking (COG-complex) CDG.
Underestimating the danger of intercurrent illness and episodic hyperthermia, which can precipitate rapid deterioration.
Overlooking cardiac and hepatic surveillance because attention is focused on the neurological phenotype.
Failing to test the wider COG complex when one subunit is normal, since several subunits produce overlapping phenotypes.
references: Standard textbook of inherited metabolic disease
Congenital disorders of glycosylation clinical and diagnostic reviews
management: No curative treatment exists; care is supportive and multidisciplinary, with early palliative planning given the high early mortality
Nutritional support for failure to thrive and feeding difficulty using nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding, and management of profound hypotonia
Hepatic care for cholestasis and hepatomegaly, including fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and correction of coagulopathy
Cardiac evaluation and supportive management of cardiac dysfunction
Heightened vigilance during febrile illness with prompt treatment of intercurrent infection and active management of episodic hyperthermia
Monitoring of liver function, coagulation, cardiac status and development, with anticonvulsants for seizures
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive COG7 disorder, with carrier testing and prenatal or preimplantation options for the family
